confusion: The cross product is ANTI-COMMUTATIVE: a × b = −(b × a). This is the opposite of the dot product. Reversing the order flips the direction.
The cross product is only defined for 3D vectors. There is no standard cross product in 2D or in dimensions other than 3 (and 7).
If a × b = 0, the vectors are parallel (or one is zero), NOT that one vector is zero. This is different from the dot product where zero means perpendicular.
The cross product result is a VECTOR perpendicular to the plane of a and b. Do not confuse its magnitude |a × b| with the dot product a · b.
The cross product is NOT associative: a × (b × c) ≠ (a × b) × c. The vector triple product expansion a × (b × c) = (a · c)b − (a · b)c must be used.
The cross product of two vectors gives a vector perpendicular to the PLANE containing both vectors. Do not think of it as a scalar area — the magnitude is the area, but the result itself is a vector.

universalFacts: The magnitude of the cross product equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors. Half of this gives the triangle area.
The cross product is fundamental in physics for describing rotational phenomena: torque, angular momentum, and magnetic force all use it.
The vector triple product identity: a × (b × c) = (a · c)b − (a · b)c (mnemonic: 'bac minus cab').
In 3D, the cross product of two vectors is unique up to a sign — it is the only binary operation on vectors that produces a perpendicular vector.
The cross product is directly related to the determinant: the scalar triple product a·(b×c) equals the determinant of the matrix with rows a, b, c.
